source_text:
αὐτοῖς ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας πλευρᾶς ὕδατι συμμιγὲς τὸ ἴδιον συνανέβλυσε αἷμα, διανυττόντων
αὐτὸν τῇ λόγχῃ τῶν τοῦ Πιλάτου στρατιωτῶν. Πᾶσαν τὴν ἱστορίαν παράγει τὴν ἐν τοῖς
ἀριθμοῖς διδάσκων ὅτι ἐν τῇ νεφέλῃ καὶ τῇ θαλάσσῃ βεβαπτισμένοι, καὶ τῶν τροφῶν
τῶν πνευματικῶν ἀξιωθέντες, ἐπειδὴ συνέφαγον τοῖς εἰδωλολάτραις, ὠλίσθησαν. τὸ δὲ
ἀνέστησαν παίζειν, ἀντὶ τοῦ πορνεύειν μετὰ τῶν μαδιανιτῶν γυναικῶν.
Συνείδησιν δὲ λέγω οὐχὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀλλὰ τὴν τοῦ ἑτέρου. ∆ιὰ τὴν συνείδησιν
οὖν ἀφεκτέον ὧν ἀφεκτέον. συνείδησιν δὲ λέγω οὐχὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ· γνωστικὴ γάρ· ἀλλὰ
τὴν τοῦ ἑτέρου, ἵνα μὴ κακῶς οἰκοδομηθῇ ἀμαθίαν μιμούμενος ὃ μὴ γινώκη
καταφρονητὴς ἀντὶ μεγαλόφρονος γινόμενος. ΤΟΜΟΣ ∆ ΛΟΓΟΣ ∆. Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς εἰδέναι
ὅτι παντὸς ἀνδρὸς ἡ κεφαλὴ ὁ Χριστός ἐστιν. Ἐπειδή τινες τῶν ἐν Κορίνθῳ νεοπαγεῖς
τὸν τῆς προσευχῆς ἀγνοοῦντες τρόπον εἰσοικισάμενοι μὲν τὴν πίστιν, οὐ μὴν ἔτι καὶ
ἠκριβωκότες τίνα χρὴ τρόπον εἰς οἶκον ἰέναι Θεοῦ· προσῄεσαν μὲν προσευξόμενοι τῷ
Θεῷ καὶ τὰς ὑπέρ γε σφῶν αὐτῶν προσκομίσαντες λιτὰς, εἶτα τοῦτο εὑρὼν ἐν
ἀκαλλεστάτῳ σχήματι· ἄνδρες γὰρ τῶν ἐξ ἔθους περιβλημάτων οὐκ ἀπογυμνοῦντες τὰς
κεφαλὰς ἐποιοῦντο τὴν πρόσοδον, γύναια δὲ ὁμοίως ἀκατασκίαστόν τε καὶ ἀναμφίε 281
στον ἔχοντα τὴν τρίχα προσῄεσαν τῷ Θεῷ, μονονουχὶ καταβοώσης ἀμφοῖν τῆς φύσεως·
δεδώρηται γὰρ ἀνδρὶ μὲν τὴν παῤῥησίαν, αἰδοῖ δὲ τὸ γύναιον συστέλλει πρὸς
εὐκοσμίαν. ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἦν ἀκόλουθον λογισμοῖς αὐτοὺς ἀναγκαίοις ἐκδυσωπεῖν εἴς γε τὸ
δεῖν ἑλέσθαι φρονεῖν ἃ χρὴ, καὶ οἱονεί τινα βραβευτὴν τοῦ ἑκατέρῳ πρέποντος τὸν τῆς
φύσεως ποιεῖσθαι νόμον, πειρᾶται ὁ Παῦλος ἐκ τοῦ φυσικοῦ νόμου πεῖσαι φρονεῖν ἃ
χρὴ, καὶ ἄνεισιν ἐπὶ τὴν ἐν ἀρχαῖς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ποίησιν. κεφαλὴν ἐνθάδε φησὶ τὸ
ἀρχέτυπον κάλλος, οὗ τὴν εἰκόνα καταπλουτούντων ὠνομασμένων ἕκαστον νοοῖτ' ἂν
εἰκότως, καὶ οὐσιώδη πως τὸν τῆς εὐγενείας, εἴτ' οὖν ἑτέρως ὁμοφυΐας,
διακληρώσασθαι τρόπον. γέγονε μὲν γὰρ ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος, τουτέστιν Ἀδὰμ, κατ'
εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν Θεοῦ· οὕτως γάρ που φησὶν ὁ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργός "Ὅτι ἐν εἰκόνι
Θεοῦ ἐποίησα τὸν ἄνθρωπον." οὐκοῦν ἀνδρὸς ἡ κεφαλὴ ὁ Χριστὸς, ἀρχέτυπος μὲν ὡς
Θεὸς, φύσεως δὲ νόμῳ τῆς καθ' ἡμᾶς καὶ ὁμοειδὴς ὅτε πέφηνεν ἄνθρωπος, καίτοι Θεὸς
ὢν ὁ Λόγος, καὶ γοῦν υἱὸν ἑαυτὸν ἀνθρώπου κατονομάζεται πανταχοῦ καίτοι τὴν ἐκ
Θεοῦ Πατρὸς γέννησιν ἀπόῤῥητον ἔχων· γέγονε λοιπὸν κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν
ἀνθρώπου τουτέστιν Ἀδὰμ ἡ γυνὴ, ἔκφυλος δὲ οὐδαμῶς, ὁμοφυὴς δὲ μᾶλλον καὶ
ὁμοειδὴς αὐτῷ· καὶ τοῦτο αὐτὸς διωμολόγηκεν ἐναργῶς ὁ προπάτωρ Ἀδὰμ φήσας
"Τοῦτο νῦν "ὀστοῦν ἐκ τῶν ὀστῶν μου καὶ σὰρξ ἐκ τῆς σαρκός μου," καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. Ἐπειδὴ
δέ τινες γενητὸν λέγουσι τὸν Υἱὸν, ὡς καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ κτίσματα, ὧν, φησὶν, ἐστὶ κεφαλὴ ὁ
Χριστός· κεφαλὴ γὰρ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς ὁ Χριστός· διενθυμεῖσθαι δεῖ καὶ πρό γε 282 τῶν
ἄλλων αὐτοὺς ὅτι τῆς βλασφημίας ἡ δύναμις, οὐ τῆς ἐφ' Υἱῷ θεωρίας ἅψεται μόνης,
διελάσει δὲ ὥσπερ ἀσχέτῳ διάττουσα δρόμῳ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν Πατέρα· καὶ τίνα τρόπον,
ἐρῶ. Εἰ γὰρ εἶναι γενητόν φασιν, καὶ τοῖς κτίσμασιν ἐναρίθμιον ἡγεῖσθαι πρέπειν τὸν ἐκ
Θεοῦ Πατρὸς Λόγον, ἐπείπερ ἐστὶ κεφαλὴ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς, πῶς οὐκ ἂν νοοῖτο κατὰ τὸν
ἴσον τρόπον κτιστὸς καὶ πεποιημένος ὑπάρχειν καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Πατὴρ, εἴπερ ἐστὶ κεφαλὴ
τοῦ Υἱοῦ σχέσιν ἔχοντος οὐσιώδη τὴν πρὸς ἡμᾶς, ἤτοι πρὸς κτίσματα; ὡς γὰρ αὐτοί
φασι, πάντη τε καὶ πάντως ἡ κεφαλὴ τῷ λοιπῷ σώματι φυσικοῖς εἰς ταυτότητα
συνδεῖται νόμοις· οὐκοῦν ὡς διὰ μέσου τοῦ Υἱοῦ, καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἥξει τὸν Θεὸν καὶ
Πατέρα τὸ πρὸς πάντα ἄνδρα συγγενές· πῶς οὖν ἔτι τὴν τῶν γεγονότων ὑπερνήχεται
φύσιν; ἢ τίνα ζητήσωμεν τὸν ὅλων ∆ημιουργόν; ἀλλ' οὐ ταῖς ἐκείνων ἀβελτερίαις
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing u03-rem-close, ‘who also for us’] ourselves (αὐτοῖς), from his own side (πλευρά), mixed with water (συμμιγές), his own blood gushed up together (συναναβλύζω), the soldiers of Pilate piercing him through (διανύττω) with the spear (λόγχη). The whole story in Numbers he brings forward (παράγει), teaching that those baptized in the cloud and the sea, and deemed worthy of the spiritual foods, since they ate together with the idolaters, slipped (ὀλισθαίνω). And the ‘they rose up to play’ is in place of (ἀντὶ τοῦ) fornicating (πορνεύειν) with the Midianite women. [Lemma] Conscience I say, not that of oneself but that of the other. On account of the conscience, then, there must be abstaining (ἀφεκτέον) from what must be abstained from. Conscience I say not one’s own — for knowing (γνωστική, that of the one with knowledge) it is — but that of the other, so that he not be badly built up (οἰκοδομηθῇ), imitating in ignorance (ἀμαθία) what he does not know, becoming a despiser (καταφρονητής) instead of great-minded (μεγαλόφρων). [Heading] Tome 4, Discourse 4. [Lemma] I want you to know that of every man the head is Christ. Since some of those in Corinth, newly fixed (νεοπαγεῖς), not knowing the manner of prayer, having housed the faith within (εἰσοικίζομαι), yet not having learned precisely in what manner one must go into the house of God: they were approaching to pray to God and bringing petitions (λιταί) on their own behalf, then [he] finding this in a most unlovely form; for men, not stripping their heads of the customary coverings, were making the approach (πρόσοδος), and little women likewise, having the hair unshaded and unclothed, were approaching God, nature all but crying out against (καταβοάω) both; for she has granted to man openness (παρρησία), but contracts (συστέλλω) the woman by shame-modesty (αἰδώς) toward good order (εὐκοσμία). And since it was consequent to put them out of countenance (ἐκδυσωπέω) by necessary reasonings toward needing to choose to think what is due, and to make the law of nature as it were an umpire (βραβευτής) of what befits each, Paul tries from the natural law to persuade to think what is due, and goes up to the making of man in the beginnings. Head here he calls the archetypal beauty, of which each of the named ones, enriched with the image, might reasonably be thought to have received by lot (διακληρόομαι), in some way essential (οὐσιώδης), the manner of good birth (εὐγένεια), or otherwise (ἑτέρως) of sameness of nature (ὁμοφυΐα). For the first man, that is Adam, came to be according to image and likeness of God; for so somewhere says the craftsman of all: ‘Because in an image of God I made man.’ So of man the head is Christ, archetype as God, but by law of the nature that is ours also of same form (ὁμοειδής) when he appeared a man, although being God the Word; and indeed he names himself son of man everywhere, although having the birth from God the Father unspeakable (ἀπόρρητος). Then came to be according to image and likeness of man, that is Adam, the woman, of other stock (ἔκφυλος) in no way, of same nature rather and same form with him; and this the forefather Adam himself confessed clearly, saying, ‘This now bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh,’ and the rest. And since some say the Son is originated (γενητός), as also the rest of the creatures, of which, he says, Christ is head — for head of every man is Christ — they must ponder (διενθυμέομαι), and before the others, that the power of the blasphemy will touch not only the contemplation (θεωρία) about the Son, but will drive through (διελαύνω), darting as in an unchecked (ἄσχετος) course, also into the Father himself; and in what manner, I will say. For if they say the Word from God the Father is originated, and that it befits to reckon him numbered among (ἐναρίθμιος) the creatures, since he is head of every man, how would not in the equal manner the Father himself be thought to be created and made, if indeed he is head of the Son, who has an essential relation (σχέσις οὐσιώδης) toward us, that is toward creatures? For as they say, in every way and wholly the head is bound together to the rest of the body by natural laws into identity (ταυτότης); then as through the middle of the Son, into God and Father himself will come the kinship toward every man; how then does he still swim above (ὑπερνήχομαι) the nature of things that came to be? Or whom shall we seek as the Creator of all? But not their stupidities (ἀβελτερία) [sentence finished at the start of u04-rem-early].
pass_b_english: …for our very selves, made his own blood gush out from his own side, mingled with water, when the soldiers of Pilate pierced him with the spear (John 19:34).

He brings forward the whole story in Numbers, teaching that those who had been baptized in the cloud and in the sea, and had been counted worthy of the spiritual food, slipped because they ate with the idolaters (1 Corinthians 10:2–5; Numbers 25:1–2). And “they rose up to play” stands for committing fornication with the Midianite women (1 Corinthians 10:7–8; compare Numbers 25:6).
“Conscience, I mean, not one’s own, but the other’s” (1 Corinthians 10:29).

So for conscience’ sake one must abstain from what one ought to abstain from. And by conscience I mean not one’s own, for one’s own is the conscience of the one with knowledge, but the other’s, so that he may not be built up in the wrong way (compare 1 Corinthians 8:10), copying in his ignorance what he does not understand, and so become a man who despises instead of a man of great soul.
“But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

Some of those in Corinth were newly established in the faith and did not know the right manner of prayer. They had given the faith a home in themselves, but they had not yet learned exactly how one ought to enter the house of God. They came to pray to God and to offer their petitions for themselves, and then Paul found this being done in a most unseemly form. For the men made their approach without uncovering their heads of their customary coverings, and the women likewise came before God with their hair unshaded and uncovered, while nature all but cried out against them both. For nature has given openness to the man, while by modesty it draws the woman in toward seemliness.

Since it was right that he should put them to shame with compelling arguments, so that they would choose to think as they ought, and that he should make the law of nature a kind of umpire of what befits each, Paul tries to persuade them from the natural law to think as they ought, and he goes back to the making of man in the beginning.

By “head” he here means the archetypal beauty. Each of those named here, being enriched with its image, may rightly be understood to have received as a portion a kind of noble descent that in some way belongs to their very being, or, to put it another way, a sameness of nature.

For the first man, that is, Adam, came into being according to the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), for so the Creator of all says somewhere: “For in the image of God I made man” (Genesis 9:6). So the head of man is Christ: the archetype as God, and also of the same form with us by the law of our nature when he appeared as man, although the Word is God. Indeed, everywhere he calls himself Son of Man, although his birth from God the Father is beyond words.

Then the woman came into being according to the image and likeness of man, that is, of Adam. She is in no way of a different stock, but rather of one nature and one form with him. And the forefather Adam himself plainly confessed this when he said, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” and what follows (Genesis 2:23).

Some say that the Son has come into being, like the rest of the creatures, of which, they say, Christ is the head, “for the head of every man is Christ.” Before anything else they must consider that the force of their blasphemy will not touch only their teaching about the Son, but, rushing on as in an unchecked course, will drive right through to the Father himself. And how, I will tell.

For if they say that the Word who is from God the Father has come into being, and that it is right to count him among the creatures because he is the head of every man, how would the Father himself not be thought, in the same way, to be created and made, if indeed he is the head of a Son who is related by his very being to us, that is, to creatures (1 Corinthians 11:3)? For, as they themselves say, the head is in every way and altogether bound to the rest of the body by natural laws, so as to be one and the same with it. Then, by way of the Son, the kinship with every man will reach God the Father himself as well. How, then, does he still rise above the nature of things that have come into being? Or whom are we to seek as the Creator of all?

choices.why: Scholion use of ἀντὶ τοῦ + infinitive: the phrase explains what the quoted words mean. Cyril says “play” means fornication, not that they played rather than sinned.

choices.english: for one’s own is the conscience of the one with knowledge
choices.why: Feminine adjective agreeing with συνείδησις; it echoes ὁ ἔχων γνῶσιν of 1 Corinthians 8:10. Nothing to do with the Gnostic sects.

choices.english: one must abstain from what one ought to abstain from
rejected: forgive those who are to be forgiven
choices.why: Verbal adjective of ἀπέχομαι, “abstain”, not ἀφίημι.
The bare, uncovered head, as in the next section.

choices.term: Ὅτι ἐν εἰκόνι Θεοῦ ἐποίησα τὸν ἄνθρωπον
choices.english: For in the image of God I made man (Genesis 9:6)
choices.why: The wording with first-person ἐποίησα is Genesis 9:6 in the Greek Old Testament.
Single nu: originated, the Arian claim; Cyril’s answer in the next section uses ἀγένητος.
Plain English for a relation of essence; the argument is that a head shares the nature of its body.
